<!-- dynamic-currency -->
<!-- ============================================================================
     What goes in a Lightfunnels page header from 2026-09-27 onward.

     The logic now lives at hlthtrack.com/dynamic-currency.js, published from
     hlth-shopify-frontend/public/. This repo's dynamic-currency-header-block.html
     remains the SOURCE, but editing it no longer changes what pages run - it has
     to be re-copied and deployed. Do not edit the page copy to "fix" something.

     WHY defer AND NOT A PLAIN <script src>:
     a synchronous cross-origin script in <head> blocks first paint until
     hlthtrack.com answers. On 2026-09-27 that domain returned 403 for ~20
     minutes under Vercel bot mitigation; blocking would have meant blank pages
     on paid traffic instead of prices quietly falling back to GBP. Resilience
     beats the flash, so the flash is solved below instead.

     WHY THE STUB EXISTS:
     the external script hides tagged figures as its first action, which only
     prevented a flash while it was INLINE in <head>. Deferred, it runs after the
     body has painted, so a non-UK visitor would see GBP79 flip to PHP2,450 on
     the one element that decides the sale. The stub applies that same hiding
     synchronously, before any paint, and gets out of the way the moment a price
     is written.

     It carries NO prices, NO endpoints and NO country map, so it should never
     need to change when markets or logic do. That is the whole point.
============================================================================ -->
<script>
(function () {
  var HIDE = "[data-price],[data-fx-gbp]{visibility:hidden}";
  var MAX_MS = 2500;          // matches the external script's own reveal timer

  // A UK visitor already sees the right text, so hiding anything for them is a
  // pure regression - today they get no hide at all. One timezone comparison
  // catches almost every one of them; this is deliberately NOT the 105-row map,
  // which is server-side work now and must not come back into page code.
  try {
    var q = new URLSearchParams(location.search).get("country");
    if (q) { if (q.toUpperCase() === "GB") return; }
    else if ((Intl.DateTimeFormat().resolvedOptions() || {}).timeZone === "Europe/London") return;
  } catch (e) {}

  var s = document.createElement("style");
  s.setAttribute("data-dc-stub", "");
  s.textContent = HIDE;
  (document.head || document.documentElement).appendChild(s);

  var done = false;
  function reveal() {
    if (done) return;
    done = true;
    if (s.parentNode) s.parentNode.removeChild(s);
  }
  setTimeout(reveal, MAX_MS);
  window.addEventListener("error", reveal);

  // Reveal as soon as a price is actually written. Observing is attached at
  // DOMContentLoaded rather than here: the style already prevents the flash, so
  // the observer only decides WHEN to stop hiding, and attaching it late keeps
  // it off the parse path of a 1.3 MB document.
  function watch() {
    var els = document.querySelectorAll("[data-price],[data-fx-gbp]");
    if (!els.length) return reveal();          // nothing tagged: never hide
    try {
      var mo = new MutationObserver(function () { mo.disconnect(); reveal(); });
      for (var i = 0; i < els.length && i < 40; i++) {
        mo.observe(els[i], { childList: true, characterData: true, subtree: true });
      }
    } catch (e) { reveal(); }
  }
  if (document.readyState === "loading") {
    document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", watch);
  } else { watch(); }
})();
</script>
<script src="https://hlthtrack.com/dynamic-currency.js" defer></script>

10 Reasons I Ditched My £500 Smartwatch For a £79 Band To Track My Workouts.

For three years I thought my £500 smartwatch made me serious about training.

Then I noticed something I couldn't unsee.  

The pro runners, cyclists, footballers. Not one wore a smartwatch. 

But many of them wore something else. A small band with no screen.

That made me almost angry. 

I'd spent nearly £500, and the fittest people alive wouldn't touch what was on my wrist.

Turns out the screen is the problem. It hogs the battery. So the watch checks your heart less, to save power. That means worse data. 

A screenless band has no screen to feed, so it reads you all the time, even mid-sprint.More readings. Fewer gaps. Data you can trust.

That £79 band does everything my £500 watch never could. Here are the 10 reasons I'll never strap a screen to my wrist again.
Note: Read this BEFORE you buy your next fitness watch.
Daniel Whitmore
Health tracking enthusiast
1. No Screen Means Better Data

My watch only read my heart now and then. To keep that big screen alive, it had to.


This band has no screen. So nothing competes for the power.


It reads me constantly, even at full sprint when my heart rate is climbing by the second. More readings means real data mid-workout, not a rough guess stitched together after the fact.
👉
See why screenless wins
2. I Forget I'm Even Wearing It

My smartwatch was a chunky slab bouncing on my wrist through every set and every mile. Heavy. Sweaty. I felt it the whole session. 


This is slim and light. I forget it's there. 


Lifting, running, even asleep. So it never comes off. And it never stops tracking.
👉
See it in action
3. It Tracks My Recovery, Not Just My Workout

My watch was dead on the charger every night. The one window where your body actually rebuilds, and it tracked nothing.


This stays on all night. It shows me my light, deep, and REM sleep, with a recovery score waiting for me in the morning.


Now I know when to push hard and when to back off. That alone made me a better trainer.
👉
See how it tracks recovery
4. It Cost Me £79, Not £500

Here's the maths that sold me. The "serious" training watches run close to £500. 


This was £79. Once.  


It tracks my workouts better than that watch ever did, for a fifth of the price. I felt daft for what I'd spent before.
5. One Charge Lasts a Month

My smartwatch died by the evening, sometimes halfway through a session. Nothing wrecks your data like a flat battery on leg day.


This lasts over 30 days on a single charge.


I plug it in for a couple of hours a month and forget about it. No nightly ritual. No dead tracker when I need it most.

6. It Tracks My Fitness All Day, Not Just the Hour I Train

Your fitness isn't the 60 minutes in the gym. It's the other 23 hours too.


This reads me around the clock. Resting heart rate, daily strain, steps, even stress.


So I finally see how my training is changing my body, day by day, not just during the workout itself.
7. Built With Doctors, Not Just Designers

Most fitness gadgets are built by tech firms chasing the flashiest screen.


This one was built alongside doctors and health experts who cared about the readings, not the looks.


It's a wellness and fitness device, not a medical tool. But the people behind it know exactly what good data should look like.
8. I Watch My Heart Get Fitter

My old watch gave me a heart rate number and not much else.

This shows me the metrics that prove the training is working. My resting heart rate dropping. My HRV climbing. My heart getting stronger week by week. 

Watching those numbers move in the right direction is what keeps me showing up.
9. The Reviews Are Crazy Good

I'm a sceptic. I read every review before I spend a penny.  

Thousands of people rate it Excellent. People who train, recover better, and finally trust their data.

That's what tipped me over the edge.
